tips.text: Formations are strongest when their flanks are protected.
High ground improves your ability to control an engagement.
Keep reserve troops behind the main line to respond to breakthroughs.
Cavalry is most effective when attacking exposed flanks or isolated units.
Avoid sending cavalry directly into prepared infantry formations.
Archers perform best when protected from direct melee combat.
Terrain can be as important as numbers. Use forests, hills, and narrow passages to your advantage.
A formation that becomes scattered is easier to surround and destroy.
Exhausted troops are less effective. Allow units time to recover when possible.
Protect your commander. Losing leadership at the wrong moment can decide a battle.
Direct commander control can help turn a critical fight, but exposes your commander to greater danger.
A well-defended position is one the enemy has not yet discovered a ridiculous way around.
Never underestimate the tactical value of looking busy while someone else carries the stone.
Cavalry can arrive quickly. Whether they should have arrived there is another question.
A commander who personally investigates every problem soon becomes one of them.
Walls are excellent defenses until someone remembers gates exist.
If your formation looks impressive from a distance, you are at least halfway to military competence.
The enemy cannot predict your strategy if you have forgotten it yourself.
Every supply shortage begins with someone saying, “We probably have enough.”
War elephants are powerful, disciplined weapons of war, right up until they have an opinion.
History remembers the victorious general. The quartermaster remembers who forgot to bring food.
Use patrol orders to secure roads, settlements, and vulnerable resource routes.
Workers are valuable strategic assets. Do not leave them exposed near the front.
Stockpiles shorten resource delivery routes and improve economic efficiency.
Building near resources can reduce the amount of time workers spend carrying supplies.
A strong economy cannot help you if the enemy cuts the road between it and your army.
Repairing damaged defenses before the next attack is usually cheaper than rebuilding them afterward.
Capturing useful infrastructure can be more valuable than destroying it.
Watch your supply routes when advancing deep into hostile territory.
War elephants can disrupt formations, but unsupported elephants can quickly become isolated.
Wildlife may react unpredictably to nearby troops and fighting.
Wolves are considerably less impressed by military rank than your soldiers are.
Scout unfamiliar terrain before committing your main force.
Keep an escape route available when fighting near rivers, cliffs, or narrow passages.
A retreat made early can preserve an army. A retreat made late can become a rout.
Concentrating your forces can overwhelm a stronger enemy fighting in separate groups.
Do not chase fleeing enemies so far that your own formation collapses.
An army marches on its stomach. The stomach, regrettably, also requires a supply line.
Enemy reinforcements are much less dangerous when they never reach the battlefield.
Every commander has a plan until a sheep joins the formation.
Destroying an enemy army is useful. Preventing it from fighting effectively is often enough.
Infantry can hold ground that faster units may struggle to defend.
Keep ranged troops away from routes enemy cavalry can reach quickly.
Battles are often decided before contact through positioning, preparation, and logistics.
A narrow front can prevent a numerically superior enemy from using all of its troops at once.
When defending, force the enemy to come to you under unfavorable conditions.
When attacking, look for weak points rather than spreading damage evenly across the enemy line.
A unit surrounded on several sides will struggle even if it began the fight at full strength.
The Iron Sepulcher is best approached with troops prepared for an unexpected engagement.
Clearing a dangerous area is not the same as securing it. Check what remains nearby.
The shortest path between two points is rarely the route selected by an army.
